title: Falls and Frailty in Older Adults
lead: Falls are not a normal part of ageing. Many are preventable with the right exercise.

blocks.text: A fall is an unexpected event in which a person comes to rest on the ground or a lower level. Falls in older adults lead to fractures, head injury, fear of falling, loss of independence and admission to care. **Frailty** is a state of reduced physiological reserve, making a person vulnerable to small stressors. **Sarcopenia** is age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. Falls usually result from several interacting risk factors.

rows: Weakness, poor balance, gait problems, previous falls, vision loss, cognitive impairment, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, foot problems, urinary urgency
Sedatives, antidepressants, antihypertensives, many medications together (polypharmacy)
Poor lighting, rugs, stairs without rails, slippery bathrooms, unsuitable footwear

sections.title: B to C. Presentation and questions

blocks.text: Ask every older adult: "Have you fallen in the past year? How many times? Do you feel unsteady? Do you worry about falling?" For each fall: where, when, what happened, any warning (dizziness, blackout, palpitations), could you get up, how long on the floor, injuries.

blocks.label: TEACHER'S VOICE
body: A fall with loss of consciousness, palpitations or chest pain is a possible syncope and needs medical assessment for cardiac causes. Do not treat it only as a balance problem.

rows: Rise from a chair, walk 3 m, turn, return, sit
Longer times indicate higher falls risk; use alongside other findings [Ref – to verify cut-offs]
Number of full stands with arms crossed
Feet together, semi-tandem, tandem, single leg; 10 s each
Unable to hold tandem 10 s: increased risk
Slow speed indicates frailty and risk
Lie 5 min, stand, measure at 1 and 3 min
Systolic drop of 20 mmHg or more, or diastolic of 10 or more: orthostatic hypotension

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Fall with blackout, palpitations, chest pain
Hip pain and inability to bear weight after a fall
Long lie (on the floor for over an hour)
Sudden new unsteadiness with neurological signs

steps: **Screen:** falls in the last year, unsteadiness, fear.
**Positive screen:** multifactorial assessment (strength, balance, gait, BP, medications, vision, feet, home, cognition).
**Refer** for medication review, vision, cardiovascular assessment as needed.
**Prescribe** progressive strength and balance exercise plus home safety changes.

blocks.text: Exercise that challenges balance, done regularly and for long enough, reduces falls [Ref – to verify Cochrane]. A widely used program is the **Otago Exercise Programme** [Ref – to verify].

rows: Sit-to-stand, knee extension with ankle weights, hip abduction in standing, heel and toe raises
2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12, 3 times a week, progress load
Tandem stance, tandem walk, single-leg stance with support, stepping in different directions, walking and turning, backward walking
Daily practice, progressing to less hand support
Practise getting up from the floor
Often recommended at least about 3 hours per week, sustained for months [Ref – to verify]

blocks.text: Progression: reduce hand support, narrow the base, add head turns, add a cognitive task, increase repetitions and load.
Other measures: footwear advice, home hazard modification, personal alarm, vitamin D and bone health review through the doctor, continence management.
TUG, 30 s chair stand, balance tests, FES-I, falls diary.

items: **What type of exercise reduces falls?** Exercise that challenges balance, combined with strength training, done long term.
**What is orthostatic hypotension?** A drop in BP on standing (systolic 20 mmHg or diastolic 10 mmHg or more).
**Why teach floor recovery?** To prevent long lies and their complications.
**What should you do if a fall involved blackout?** Medical assessment for cardiac or neurological causes.
**Why assess fear of falling?** Fear leads to inactivity, weakness and more falls.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Interpret TUG, chair stand, balance tests and lying-standing BP.
Prescribe and progress strength and balance training.
